storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — radar is clear, there is no thunderstorm fuel in the air and no weather alerts are out, so the cove gets the same quiet, mild evening as the surrounding towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No Sound buffer tonight: the 64°F water is only about 4°F cooler than the air at 4 PM — already under the ~5°F protective threshold — and by 7 PM the air is slightly cooler than the water; moot with nothing on radar.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: a light southerly flow covers the area under mostly sunny skies. The 3:44 PM radar scan showed no rain or storm cells anywhere in range, the model has zero storm fuel (the instability measure forecasters call CAPE is 0 through the evening), and there are no National Weather Service alerts in effect. Stations around the cove are reading about 68°F with no rain.

Local effect — neutral: on storm days the cool Sound can lay a stable layer of air over the water that weakens incoming storms, but it needs the air to be at least about 5°F warmer than the water. At 4 PM that gap is only about 4°F (68°F air over 64°F water), so there is no meaningful buffer even now. It shrinks further from here: the Sound holds its temperature while the air cools toward sunset (6:16 PM), so the gap is about 3°F at 5 PM, under 1°F by 6 PM, and by 7 PM the air is about 1°F cooler than the water.

No sea breeze either: the southerly wind is the background (gradient) wind, not a sea breeze — the land is not warm enough relative to the water to drive one, and only about half the coastal stations are southerly. The winds higher up are fairly strong from the west, which on a storm day would help organised storms push through to the coast, but with no storms and no fuel that has nothing to act on tonight.

Most likely outcome for the cove: dry through the evening, with temperatures sliding from about 67°F at 5 PM to the low 60s by 7 PM and the light southerly easing after dark. No difference between the cove and inland towns — there is nothing for the Sound to help or hurt.

What would change the call: very little tonight. The next storm chance the National Weather Service flags is a strong cold front Thursday night into Friday, bringing showers and a slight chance of a thunderstorm Friday afternoon — likely a narrow band of showers with a few thunderstorms along the front. Forecasters say it is too early to judge any severe threat.

wind.tactics_blurb: A light southerly straight up the cove — about 6 kt at 5 PM, easing to 4–5 kt around sunset and staying light after dark. No side pays reliably: start mid-line, sail the middle and play the small oscillations; if the wind eases left toward south-southeast, lean to the west side of the course, away from the Greenwich Point wind shadow.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of wind day: a light gradient wind — the breeze comes from the large-scale weather pattern, and no sea breeze is in play. A sea breeze needs the land to be roughly 5°F warmer than the water; today the air–water temperature difference is only 3.8°F (68°F air, 64°F Sound), and just over half the coastal stations (11 of 20) are southerly. The well-sited airport anemometers average 7.7 kt, right at the line between light and moderate; with the model fading the wind through the window, this is treated as a light-wind evening.

Through the window: at 4 PM Riverside Yacht Club was reading south-southwest (202°) at 4 kt, averaging 7 kt over ten minutes and gusting 10; the mid-Sound buoy had a steadier south 11 gusting 15. Expect about 6 kt from the south at 5 PM, easing to 4–5 kt around sunset at 6:16 PM and holding at 3–4 kt after dark. A gradient wind does not die with the sun the way a sea breeze does, but one this light loses a knot or two as the evening air cools and settles. Model data stops at 7 PM in this run, so the 8–10 PM rows carry the 7 PM wind forward and should be read as estimates.

Model versus the cove: the model and the stations disagree on direction. For 4 PM the model had southeast (142°) at 6 kt, while western Sound stations sit at south-southwest (197°) — about 55° further right. Speeds agree. The table uses the observed direction as the baseline and follows the model's slow drift left into the evening, landing on due south rather than the model's south-southeast (155–165°). This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day, so the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply.

Where the pressure is and how it shifts: a due-south wind runs straight up the cove axis — the cleanest, steadiest direction here, with fairly even pressure across the course and a little more breeze toward the mouth. Shifts should be small gust-and-lull oscillations rather than a one-way trend, so play them from the middle. The thing to watch is the slow drift left: if the wind gets round to south-southeast, Greenwich Point starts to shelter the east side, which goes lighter and shiftier, and the west side of the course carries more pressure.

What it feels like: light-air racing — 6 kt with puffs near 10 at the start of the window is the best of it, good for one-design dinghies. From sunset on it is 4–5 kt and under, drifter conditions where keeping the boat moving matters more than the shifts, and a race committee may shorten course. Mostly sunny and about 67°F at 5 PM, cooling to the low 60s by 7 PM.

data_caveats: HRRR model run only reached 7 PM (forecast hours 5–12 unavailable) — the 8, 9 and 10 PM wind rows are carried forward from the 7 PM value, not model output.

Model and stations disagree on wind direction: the model had southeast (142°) for 4 PM while western Sound stations read south-southwest (197°) — table directions are based on the observations, eased left with the model's trend.
Gust figures are estimates scaled from sustained wind and current station gusts — the model feed has no gust field.
Wind-regime call is borderline: airport stations average 7.7 kt, right at the light/moderate line.
Western Long Island Sound buoy 44040 reading is 75 minutes old; water temperature is from Bridgeport Harbor.
National Weather Service forecast text covers this afternoon only — the evening call rests on current observations and the model.
